Parse the answer and check each claim against the passage that its anchor cites. A claim without an anchor, or with an anchor whose passage does not state the claim, is dropped or sent back for a re-ask. An answer that slipped past the score gate then cannot ship a claim that its cited passage does not support.

### How to measure it

- **Refusal calibration.** On a set of questions with no answer in the store, the share that the system refuses.
- **False confidence rate.** The share of those questions that got an answer anyway.
- **Wrong refusal rate.** On in-corpus questions, the share refused. A threshold that is too high fails here.

Move the threshold on the held-out set, never on production anecdotes, and re-tune it when the embedder, the reranker or the corpus changes.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Where does the threshold come from? Expected: the distribution of rank-1 scores on a held-out set with known in-corpus and out-of-corpus questions; it is specific to the corpus.
- **Level 3:** What does the generator prompt need beyond "use only the context"? Expected: cite each claim with its anchor and say it does not know when the snippets do not answer; the explicit instruction cut hallucination by 40 to 60 percent in the question answering lesson.
- **Level 4:** Too many refusals are also a failure. How do you balance it? Expected: track the false confidence rate on out-of-corpus questions next to the wrong refusal rate on in-corpus questions, and move the threshold on the held-out set.
- **Level 4:** How does the citation post-filter work with the refusal gate? Expected: each claim is checked against the passage its anchor cites, and a claim with no anchor or with a passage that does not state it is dropped or re-asked, so a weak answer that passed the score gate cannot ship an unsupported claim.
questions.wrong:
- "Tell the model to be careful." An instruction cannot see the retrieval scores; the first gate belongs before generation.
- "Refuse when retrieval returns fewer than k chunks." A count is not confidence; weak chunks still fill k slots.
- "Set the threshold once from the fixture." It is corpus specific and moves when the embedder, the reranker or the corpus changes.

questions.title: Pick how many candidates the reranker scores
questions.prompt: You add a cross-encoder behind a hybrid retriever. The prompt receives K chunks. The team wants a rule for N, the number of candidates the reranker scores, and one engineer proposes a small N to protect the latency budget. How do you choose N, and what do you refuse?
questions.short: Choose N from the recall curve of the reranked output and the latency budget together. Sweep N on a held-out query set; the lift saturates at a knee somewhere around 20 to 50 candidates, and past it every extra candidate costs a forward pass for nothing. Keep N at least three times K, because the reranker can only promote a chunk that the retriever put in the pool.
questions.full:
### The one tunable

The two-stage pipeline has one knob. The bi-encoder returns N candidates, the cross-encoder scores each pair and keeps K. The lesson shows the shape of the curve with illustrative values: recall at 1 rises from N of 5 to N of 20, rises less to N of 50, and does not change at N of 100. The values are not measurements from the fixture; the knee is real.

### The cap

The cross-encoder cannot raise recall above the bi-encoder recall at N. A low N caps quality, not only latency. If N equals K, the reranker can reorder the K candidates but cannot bring a new one in, so recall at K cannot move and the lift looks like zero.

### The cost side

- Batch the N pairs into one forward pass. Scored one by one, the latency multiplies by N.
- Plan the memory. A 22M parameter cross-encoder takes 88 MB at float32 before any batch.
- Cache reranker output by the hash of the query and the document id. A stable corpus reranks the same way, so hits buy a free latency cut.

### Pin the three together

The bi-encoder, the cross-encoder and N are one choice. A change in any of them invalidates the eval, so the sweep runs again after a model change.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why does the curve flatten? Expected: past the knee the extra candidates are rarely relevant, so the reranker has nothing more to promote while each one still costs a forward pass.
- **Level 3:** You cut N from 50 to 10 to save latency. What else moves? Expected: the recall cap, because the reranker cannot see a chunk outside the pool; run the eval again instead of assuming.
- **Level 4:** The embedder is upgraded. Is the chosen N still valid? Expected: no; a new bi-encoder changes recall at N, so the sweep must run again before the release.
- **Level 4:** How do you get the latency back without a smaller N? Expected: one batched forward pass for the N pairs, and a cache keyed on the query and the document id.
questions.wrong:
- "Set N equal to K to save time." Then the reranker can only reorder the K chunks and never bring a new one in, so recall at K cannot move.
- "The larger N, the better." Past the knee the lift saturates and each extra candidate costs one forward pass.
- "Pick N once and keep it." N is pinned with the two models; a change in either one invalidates the choice.

questions.title: The reranker is perfect offline and worse in production
questions.prompt: A new cross-encoder reranker lifts MRR on the offline fixture to a near-perfect value. In production the same reranker makes the top result worse than the retriever alone. List the causes you check, in order, and say how each one shows up.
questions.short: Check the training data first: if the hand-labeled training pairs include the eval queries, the eval is a memory test and the lift is fake. Then check the pair order in production, because a cross-encoder is not symmetric and a swapped query and document collapses recall. Then check the candidate pool, because production candidates come from the real bi-encoder, and its recall at N caps what the reranker can see.
questions.full:
### Cause 1: the eval leaked into training

The reranker lesson warns that if the hand-labeled training pairs include the eval queries, the rerank looks magical. The end-to-end lesson makes the point concrete: its 14 training triples resemble the eval queries, so the demo keeps the eval queries disjoint on purpose. A leak shows as a near-perfect fixture and a production result that looks like a different model.

### Cause 2: the pair is swapped

The score for the query followed by the document is not the score for the document followed by the query. Always feed the query first. A swap shows as a collapse, not a drift, because every score is computed in the wrong direction.

### Cause 3: the pool is not the production pool

An offline fixture can hand the reranker a made-up pool that always contains the gold chunk. In production the pool comes from the bi-encoder, and the reranker cannot raise recall above the bi-encoder recall at N. The lesson's fix is to pin the bi-encoder, the cross-encoder and N together; a change in any of them invalidates the eval.

### What to log so the next one is cheaper

Log the rank-1 cross-encoder score per query. A top score below a corpus threshold marks an out-of-domain query, and a shift in the score distribution after a release marks a regression before users do.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** How do you make the leak impossible? Expected: hold the eval queries out of the training triples strictly, even on a fixture, as the end-to-end lesson does.
- **Level 2:** What does a swapped pair look like in the numbers? Expected: a collapse rather than a drift, because every score is computed for the wrong direction.
- **Level 3:** Why does a synthetic candidate pool inflate the offline result? Expected: it can contain the gold chunk every time, while the real bi-encoder's recall at N caps what the reranker sees in production.
- **Level 3:** Which one number do you log per query to catch the next regression? Expected: the rank-1 cross-encoder score; a top score below a corpus threshold marks an out-of-domain query.
questions.wrong:
- "The production model is a different build." Check the data and the inputs before the weights; a leak and a swapped pair both reproduce with the same weights.
- "The fixture is too small to mean anything." Size does not create a leak; overlap between training and eval queries does.
- "Lower N in production to match the fixture." A smaller N lowers the recall cap and makes the pipeline worse.

questions.title: Why hybrid search fuses ranks and not scores
questions.prompt: You have a BM25 ranked list and a vector ranked list for the same query. An engineer proposes to merge them as alpha times the BM25 score plus one minus alpha times the cosine. What is wrong with that, and what do you do instead?
questions.short: BM25 scores are unbounded and change with the corpus, while a cosine sits between -1 and 1, so a weighted sum needs a new alpha every time you re-index. Reciprocal rank fusion merges by rank instead: each document gets the sum, over the lists, of one over k plus its rank, with k at 60. Ranks are comparable across the two retrievers, so nothing has to be calibrated.
questions.full:
### The formula and one worked case

A document at rank 1 in the vector list and rank 5 in the BM25 list gets 1/(60+1) + 1/(60+5) = 0.0164 + 0.0154 = 0.0318. A document at rank 3 and rank 2 gets 1/(60+3) + 1/(60+2) = 0.0159 + 0.0161 = 0.0320. The second document wins by a hair: a document that is good in both lists beats one that is first in one list and deep in the other.

### What k does

With k at 60, rank 1 contributes 1/61 and rank 10 contributes 1/70. The contribution decays slowly, so deep candidates still vote. A smaller k lets the top results dominate. A larger k flattens the curve.

### Why ranks and not scores

A linear combination of scores needs an alpha tuned per corpus, and it breaks on every re-index because the BM25 score spread moves. Ranks do not have a scale. The capstone lesson notes that the rank-based baseline has beaten score interpolation in every public TREC track since 2010, and that the production search engines that document hybrid search came to the same conclusion.

### A knob that keeps the method honest

If you have evidence that one retriever beats the other on your data, multiply its rank contribution by a weight. The rank decay shape stays and the method stays scale free.
questions.followups:
- **Level 2:** What does the constant k control? Expected: how fast the contribution decays with rank; at 60, rank 1 gives 1/61 and rank 10 gives 1/70, so deep candidates still count.
- **Level 2:** When would you lower k? Expected: when the top result of each list should dominate the fused order.
- **Level 3:** You know BM25 is better on your corpus. How do you express that? Expected: a per-list weight that multiplies the rank contribution of the BM25 list; the decay shape and the scale-free property both survive.
- **Level 3:** Why does the rank method survive a re-index when the weighted sum does not? Expected: ranks keep their meaning when the corpus changes, while BM25 scores and their spread move, so the tuned alpha no longer fits.
questions.wrong:
- "Normalize both scores to a zero to one range and add them." The two distributions still differ per query and per corpus, so the tuned balance drifts after a re-index.
- "Take the document with the highest score in either list." One unbounded BM25 score then dominates every query; ranks are the comparable unit.
- "Fusion is only a tie-breaker between the two lists." In the demo it decides the top result on every query class; a document good in both lists beats one that is top in only one.

questions.title: Build the eval that picks a retrieval configuration
questions.prompt: Take-home. You receive a corpus of a few hundred internal documents and a retrieval pipeline with two chunkers and two retrievers behind flags. Build the evaluation that tells the team which configuration to ship, and write up what the numbers mean. You have one evening.
questions.short: Build a labeled query set first, stratified by query type, with gold document ids and gold answer text for each query. Run every configuration against the same set and report recall at 5 for each slice, plus MRR and the share of queries whose top 5 holds a chunk with the gold answer text, and read the spread between configurations. Label at document level so the same labels grade every chunker; if you label at chunk level, record the chunker in the qrels and relabel after any change of chunker.
questions.full:
### The deliverable

1. **A qrels file.** One record per query with the query text, the gold document ids, a graded relevance map and the gold answer substring. Label at document level, not at chunk level, so the labels survive a chunker change.
2. **A stratified set.** The chunking lesson uses a 50-query set split across factoid, analytical and multi-hop questions. Multi-hop queries reveal different winners than factoid queries, and one average hides the losing class.
3. **The run matrix.** Two chunkers times two retrievers, every cell against the same qrels, same k values.
4. **The metrics.** Recall at 5 as the primary number, precision at k beside it, MRR for the position of the first hit, nDCG if the labels are graded, and an answer hit at 5 that counts a query only when a top-five chunk contains the gold answer substring. Document-level recall cannot tell two chunkers apart when both return chunks of the gold document and only one of them returns the chunk with the answer. The answer hit measures exact-span coverage only: a multi-hop answer spread across several chunks can miss it while the top five still supports the answer, so read it beside recall and not as a full retrieval score.
5. **The report.** One table with one row per configuration and one column per slice, then a recommendation and the reason, then what you would measure next.

### What to expect

The chunking comparison lesson shows the pattern: the structural header splitter wins on markdown, semantic clustering wins on plain prose, and recursive splitting holds its own on a mixed corpus. The hybrid retriever beats the lexical baseline on recall. Your corpus decides which of these holds.

### Guards that graders look for

- The labeling level is recorded in the qrels header, and chunk-level gold ids name the chunker they were produced against.
- Any training pairs for a reranker are disjoint from the eval queries.
- The per-query results are persisted, not only the averages.
- The write-up names what this eval cannot tell: answer quality, which needs faithfulness and relevance judged by a model from another family or by hand.
questions.followups:
- **Level 3:** Why split the queries by type? Expected: factoid and multi-hop queries reveal different winners, and one average hides the class that loses.
- **Level 3:** The labels were produced with chunker A. Can you reuse them for chunker B? Expected: only if the labels are at document or span level; chunk ids change with the boundaries, so record the chunker in the qrels and relabel otherwise.
- **Level 4:** How do you justify the query count in the write-up? Expected: a 50-query stratified set for the first decision, then tiers of 20 queries in CI, 200 nightly and 2000 weekly, with a note on what each tier can and cannot detect.
- **Level 4:** What do you refuse to conclude after one evening? Expected: anything about answer quality, because the eval grades retrieval; faithfulness and relevance need a judge, and a judge from the generator's own family is biased.
questions.wrong:
- "I wrote ten questions myself and ran each configuration." Ten questions of one type cannot separate four configurations or expose a class that always misses.
- "Here is the average recall for each configuration." One average hides per-slice winners and the class that fails.
- "I changed the chunker and reused the chunk-level labels." Chunk ids no longer line up with the new chunks; label at document level, or relabel and record the chunker in the qrels header.
